title: Where Is Space Biology Going — and Where Should It?

blocks.html: A three-corpus computational map of research priorities, open data, and the published literature — with the field's temporal drift read against the programs, publications, and events that drove it, and an evidence-based hypothesis for where NASA funding should move next.

items.label: Corpora
items.value: OpenAlex · NASA OSDR · National Academies Decadal Surveys

blocks.html: Every figure in this report is a live, interactive Plotly chart — hover for exact values, zoom, pan, and toggle series in the legend. The document is fully self-contained: all charts and the plotting library are embedded, so it works offline and unchanged when the file is shared.

paras: Human deep-space exploration depends on a biological research base aligned with the risks astronauts will actually face. We ask whether that base is aligned, and in which direction it is drifting, by computationally comparing three corpora that occupy the same scientific embedding space but play different roles: the broad published literature (101,273 OpenAlex records), the open-data evidence base (171 papers deposited in NASA's Open Science Data Repository, OSDR), and the field's strategic priorities (three National Academies Decadal Survey volumes, 2,580 passages). Using SPECTER2 embeddings, HDBSCAN topic discovery, a new hierarchical-clustering capability, cross-corpus semantic probing, and per-year emphasis trajectories, we quantify the gap between what is prioritised, what has reusable data, and what is being published — and how that gap moves over three decades.

Three findings stand out. First, the gap is two-dimensional: the integrative human-physiology risks the Decadal Survey elevates — cardiovascular/fluid-shift, neuro-ocular (SANS), muscle, and (in absolute terms) bone — are not merely under-represented in the literature; their emphasis is actively falling, while omics, microbiome, and plant biology rise without a corresponding pull from priorities or open data. Second, this reorientation is invisible to paper-counting: the coarse topic composition of yearly output is broadly stable, so the shift lives in the semantic emphasis within the on-target literature. Third, the trajectories are legible against the historical record: the rises track identifiable programs and landmark results (NASA GeneLab and the 2019 Twins Study for omics; the NIH Human Microbiome Project for microbiome; the ISS Veggie and Advanced Plant Habitat for plants), while the falls track the maturation of countermeasures and infrastructure (resistive-exercise and bisphosphonate protocols for bone; the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory for radiation) rather than the resolution of the underlying risk. We synthesise the two axes into a single map and close with a hypothesis for how NASA should redistribute research funding — a hypothesis that the 2023 Decadal Survey's own finding of severe programme under-funding makes urgent. Two further analyses sharpen the picture: a theme co-occurrence network shows the retreating integrative-human-physiology risks form a single densely-connected community of co-studied problems — so their decline is one coordinated reorientation rather than ten coincidences — and an acceleration view confirms the drift has not begun to reverse in the most recent five years. Every date in the historical reading is validated against a primary source.

blocks.html:
space biology · research-gap analysis · SPECTER2 · topic modelling ·
hierarchical clustering · science of science · NASA OSDR / GeneLab · Decadal Survey · funding strategy

NASA's Moon-to-Mars programme turns a set of once-academic biological questions into
operational risks. A crew transiting to Mars will spend years beyond the protection of Earth's
magnetosphere and gravity, and every major physiological system — skeletal, cardiovascular, ocular,
muscular, immune — will be perturbed at once, with no resupply and no rapid return.

A field's research literature is not automatically aligned with its mission. Scientific attention follows many incentives — methodological fashion, data availability, publishability, the gravitational pull of adjacent biomedicine — that need not track the risks an agency most needs answered. The question this report asks is therefore practical: is the space-biology research base aligned with the priorities NASA has formally adopted, and if not, which way is it drifting?

We answer it by triangulating three different kinds of document. What the community says it should study is captured by the National Academies' Decadal Surveys. What it has produced reusable evidence for is captured by NASA's Open Science Data Repository. What it is actually publishing is captured by a large OpenAlex harvest. Because all three are embedded in the same semantic space, we can measure not only what each contains but how far apart they are — and, for the literature, how that distance has changed year by year since the mid-1990s. We then take the unusual step of interpreting those trajectories: for each rising or falling theme we ask what programme, facility, or landmark publication in the real world plausibly drove the change, and whether the change reflects a scientific advance or merely a shift in fashion. The contribution is fivefold: (i) a reusable hierarchical-clustering capability added to the analysis platform; (ii) a two-axis "priority gap × temporal momentum" framework that separates static under-service from directional drift; (iii) an event-grounded, source-validated reading of the field's three-decade reorientation; (iv) a theme co-occurrence network that resolves the field's ten risks into co-studied communities and shows the neglected human-physiology risks form a single one of them; and (v) a concrete, evidence-tied funding hypothesis.

blocks.text: Background: three windows on one field
The published literature — a broad, noisy net

blocks.html: The Space_Biology corpus is a 101,273-record harvest from OpenAlex assembled by keyword and concept queries around spaceflight, microgravity, and space life sciences. It is deliberately broad, and breadth has a cost: more than 99% of the records score near zero on a hybrid relevance measure (hybrid_favorability, a blend of keyword and semantic scoring), meaning the net catches a great deal of general biomedicine, ecology, science-education material, and bibliographic-metadata fragments alongside genuine spaceflight biology. Figure 1 shows the corpus as a two-dimensional map of its SPECTER2 embeddings; the field is an archipelago of topic islands rather than a single continent. Figure 2 shows why raw counts mislead — the favorability distribution is overwhelmingly concentrated near zero, and the true on-target core is the thin tail. The methodological lesson, which recurs throughout this report, is that the interesting signal in this corpus is not volume but emphasis.

blocks.alt: 2D UMAP map of the Space_Biology literature
blocks.headline: The literature landscape.
blocks.caption:
Each point is one of 101,273 papers, positioned
  by a 2-D UMAP projection of its 768-dimensional SPECTER2 embedding and coloured by HDBSCAN topic. The
  field resolves into many well-separated islands — biomedicine, ecology, science education, and a

blocks.alt: Histogram of hybrid favorability scores
blocks.headline: Signal versus noise.
blocks.caption: Distribution of hybrid-favorability scores across the harvest. Over 99% of records sit near zero; canonical space-biology venues (npj Microgravity, IJMS, NASA technical reports) populate the thin high-scoring tail. Any count-based reading of "how much research exists on X" is dominated by the near-zero bulk and must be corrected for relevance.

blocks.html: NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) is the field's reusable-evidence layer: studies for which raw, standardised, re-analysable spaceflight data were deposited. It incorporates the heritage GeneLab omics archive, launched in 2014 and merged with the Ames Life Sciences Data Archive in 2021 to form OSDR1 — so the corpus is, by construction, an omics-first record. Our OSDR corpus comprises 171 unique papers (8,646 text chunks). Its character is unambiguous from its journal profile (Figure 3): it is led by npj Microgravity (31 papers), followed by Scientific Reports, Nature Communications, iScience, and Microbiome. Its model-organism profile (Figure 4) is equally telling: human/clinical and rodent material dominate, followed by microbial and Arabidopsis samples, with the classic genetic models (Drosophila, C. elegans) present but minor. Titles confirm the identity — comparative transcriptomics of Arabidopsis, multi-omics of rodent and Drosophila spaceflight, the "NASA GeneLab RNA-seq consensus pipeline", ISS microbiome surveys, charged-particle radiation studies. OSDR is mechanistic, omics-first, and model-organism-centred. It represents not what the field talks about, but what it has made independently checkable — a far more demanding and therefore far smaller record.

blocks.alt: OSDR papers by journal
blocks.headline: What OSDR is.
blocks.caption: Publication venues of the 171 open-data papers. The dominance of npj Microgravity and multi-omics venues identifies OSDR as the mechanistic, data-deposited core of spaceflight biology — the evidence that can actually be re-used.

blocks.alt: OSDR mentions by model organism
blocks.headline: What OSDR studies.
blocks.caption: Mentions of major model systems across the OSDR text (summed synonym counts). Human/clinical and rodent material lead, then microbial and Arabidopsis. Note that the plant signal is Arabidopsis, the model plant — not a crop. The open-data base is built on the systems that best support molecular protocols, which shapes what can later be re-analysed.

blocks.text: The strategic priorities — the Decadal Surveys

blocks.html: The Decadal_Survey corpus is the community's formal statement of what NASA should fund. It comprises three National Academies volumes (2,580 passages):

rows.html: Recapturing a Future for Space Exploration: Life and Physical Sciences Research for a New Era (2011)
The prior decadal survey, written to rebuild a programme descoped after 2005; sets the baseline priority agenda.8
Thriving in Space: Ensuring the Future of Biological and Physical Sciences Research — A Decadal Survey for 2023–2032
The current agenda NASA is directed to pursue: 11 key questions across three themes.9
A Midterm Assessment of Implementation of the Decadal Survey on Life and Physical Sciences Research at NASA (2018)
Progress audit against the 2011 priorities.

blocks.html: These are not research papers but strategy prose: recommendations, roadmaps, and consensus priorities spanning both biological and physical sciences. That breadth matters for interpretation — the surveys weigh fluid physics, combustion, and fundamental-physics facilities alongside human physiology, so a theme's prominence here reflects its standing among all of NASA's non-astrophysics research, not biology alone. Their leading vocabulary (Figure 5) is aspirational and system-level ("physical sciences", "space exploration", "research programme"), and they repeatedly call for integrated, translational human research rather than single-system studies — a point we return to in the recommendations. The 2023 volume is also blunt about resources: it finds that NASA's Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) division is the least-funded division in the Science Mission Directorate and recommends increasing the BPS science budget roughly ten-fold within the decade — from about $85 million in FY2023 toward the ~$1 billion that would put it on a par with the Science Mission Directorate's other divisions.9 That the priorities are both demanding and starved of funds is the backdrop against which any re-allocation argument must be read.

blocks.alt: Top terms in the Decadal Survey corpus
blocks.headline: What the Decadal Survey is.
blocks.caption:
Characteristic terms across the three
  volumes. The register is strategic and cross-disciplinary rather than experimental — this is a
  statement of priorities, and physical-sciences language sits beside the biological.

blocks.title: The three-way question
paras:
Priorities (Decadal), evidence (OSDR), and literature (OpenAlex) rarely coincide. Where the
  literature is loud but priorities and open data are quiet, effort may be mis-allocated; where
  priorities are loud but literature and data are quiet, a risk may be going unmet. The rest of this
  report measures those mismatches, tracks their motion over time, and asks what in the real world
  moved them.

blocks.html: Every passage in all three corpora is embedded with SPECTER2, a scientific-document model that maps titles and abstracts to 768-dimensional vectors in which citation-and-topic neighbours lie close together. Because a single model embeds all three corpora, distances between corpora are meaningful: a Decadal recommendation and an OSDR transcriptomics paper about the same risk land in the same region of the space. This shared geometry is what makes cross-corpus comparison possible.

Within each corpus we reduce the 768-D embeddings with UMAP (to 5 dimensions for clustering and 2 for visualisation) and cluster with HDBSCAN, which discovers a data-driven number of topics and labels sparse points as noise rather than forcing them into clusters. Each resulting topic is named by its most distinctive keywords. The literature yields 288 topics; the on-target core surfaces as a space, biology, research cluster.

Flat topics hide how themes nest. We therefore added two hierarchical-clustering functions to the analysis platform, wired through its Python API, MCP tool interface, and web server so they are reusable beyond this study. Each reduces a topic to the centroid of its members' embeddings and joins topics by Ward linkage. hierarchical_dendrogram renders the resulting tree; hierarchical_cluster cuts it at a chosen height to assign every paper to a coarse "super-theme". Dendrograms expose which topics are near-synonyms and which are genuinely distant; the agglomerative cut gives a small, interpretable partition for composition analysis (§4.3).

To compare corpora on the same terms, we define ten spaceflight-risk themes (bone, muscle, cardiovascular/fluid-shift, neuro-ocular/SANS, immune, radiation/DNA, gene-expression/omics, plant/crops, microbiome, circadian/behavioural) and embed a natural-language probe for each. We combine all three corpora into one file, score every passage's cosine similarity to every theme probe (semantic_score), and average within each corpus. A theme's raw mean, however, is dominated by a baseline offset — the corpora sit at different absolute similarities (Literature 0.743 < OSDR 0.758 < Decadal 0.771) simply because strategy prose and curated abstracts are lexically denser than a broad harvest. We remove this offset by mean-centering each corpus (subtracting its own across-theme average), so the reported emphasis value answers the right question: relative to everything else this corpus discusses, how much weight does it place on this theme? Values are scaled ×1000 for readability.

Only the literature carries usable dates. (OSDR's publish_time is stored as a float and mis-parses almost entirely to the Unix epoch; the Decadal volumes have no per-passage dates.) For the literature we compute two temporal views per year from 1995–2024, the interval with adequate sample sizes: the share of each year's output falling into each super-theme (a volume measure, §4.3), and the mean semantic emphasis of each risk theme (an attention measure, §4.4). Comparing the two is itself informative. In §5 we overlay the emphasis trajectories on a hand-built timeline of programmes, facilities, and landmark publications to test whether the movements have identifiable real-world drivers.

blocks.text: The internal structure of each corpus

blocks.html: The dendrograms make each corpus's organisation legible. In the literature (Figure 6), the on-target space, biology, research topic is not a hub — it is a lone leaf that joins education, "spatial"-homonym false positives, and the biomedical/ecological bulk only at the maximum linkage distance. Because the chart is interactive, the on-target branch can be zoomed directly: the genuine core is small and surrounded by near-neighbours that are lexical accidents rather than scientific kin. This is the haystack made visible.

blocks.alt: Dendrogram of Space_Biology topics
blocks.headline: Literature hierarchy.
blocks.caption:
Ward linkage over topic centroids for the
  largest literature topics. The on-target cluster is peripheral, merging with the mass only at the far
  right. Zoom into the lower branches to inspect the on-target neighbourhood — science-education and
  "spatial"-homonym topics sit right beside the genuine core.

blocks.html: OSDR (Figure 7) tells the opposite story — a compact, coherent tree that splits cleanly into an omics/plant branch, a microgravity gene-expression branch, and a radiation/rodent branch, mirroring the mechanistic identity established in §2.2. The Decadal tree (Figure 8), re-clustered at finer resolution so its homogeneous prose resolves into more than a handful of topics, separates into human-physiology, physical-sciences, and plant branches; the prominence of the physical-sciences branch is a direct visual reminder that the survey's remit is broader than biology.

blocks.alt: Dendrogram of OSDR topics
blocks.headline: Open-data hierarchy.
blocks.caption:
OSDR's topics form a tight, well-structured tree —
  omics/plant, microgravity gene expression, and radiation/rodent branches — reflecting a curated,
  mechanistic corpus.

blocks.alt: Dendrogram of Decadal Survey topics
blocks.headline: Priorities hierarchy.
blocks.caption:
The Decadal corpus re-clustered at finer resolution
  resolves into human-physiology, physical-sciences, and plant branches. The physical-sciences branch is
  substantial — priorities are not biology-only.

blocks.html:
Cutting the literature tree into nine super-themes (Figure 9) gives the interpretable partition
used for the composition analysis below. The largest is the on-target space-biology/radiation
macro-area (~10.5k papers); plant biology forms a distinct ~3.2k super-theme; and a substantial cluster
is bibliographic-metadata noise — a partition we treat honestly rather than hide.

blocks.alt: Sizes of the nine literature super-themes
blocks.headline: Super-themes.
blocks.caption:
The nine coarse clusters produced by cutting the literature
  dendrogram, by paper count. These provide a mutually exclusive partition — each paper belongs to exactly
  one — which is what makes a share-of-output composition well defined.

blocks.text: The static gap: priorities vs. evidence vs. literature

blocks.html:
Figure 10 is the core cross-sectional result: the mean-centred emphasis of each risk theme in
all three corpora at once. Reading it theme by theme reveals a structured, non-random pattern rather
than uniform misalignment.

blocks.alt: Grouped bar of theme emphasis across three corpora
blocks.headline: The three-corpus gap.
blocks.caption:
Relative (mean-centred, ×1000) emphasis of ten
  spaceflight-risk themes in the literature, the open-data base, and the priorities. Bars above zero =
  emphasised more than that corpus's average; below zero = less. The ordering and sign disagreements
  between the three bars of each theme are the "gaps".

blocks.html: Three regimes emerge. Aligned and well-served: gene-expression/omics and immune dysregulation score high in all three corpora — the field's shared strengths. Priority-led, literature-lagging: muscle atrophy (Decadal +4.2 vs. literature −7.7), cardiovascular/fluid-shift (−6.9 vs. −17.3), neuro-ocular/SANS (−0.1 vs. −6.4), and circadian/behavioural (+8.5 vs. −5.6) are all weighted more heavily by priorities than by the literature that is supposed to address them. Literature-led, priority-light: plant/crops (literature +7.5 but Decadal −11.4 and OSDR −9.3) and microbiome (literature +0.4, Decadal −12.7) run ahead of both the strategic agenda and the open-data base.

Figure 11 distils this into a single ranking: the priority gap, Decadal emphasis minus literature emphasis, for each theme. It sorts the field cleanly. On the left, the themes priorities want more of than the literature supplies — circadian (+14.1), muscle (+11.9), cardiovascular (+10.4), immune (+9.1), SANS (+6.3); on the right, the themes the literature over-weights relative to priorities — plant/crops (−19.0), microbiome (−13.0), gene/omics and bone (−10.2 each). Radiation sits almost exactly at zero: priorities and literature agree on it. This one bar is the static half of the report's thesis.

blocks.alt: Priority minus literature gap ranked by theme
blocks.headline: The priority gap, ranked.
blocks.caption:
Decadal minus literature emphasis per theme.
  Positive (left) = priorities want more than the literature supplies (integrative human physiology,
  plus circadian); negative (right) = the literature over-invests relative to priorities (plant,
  microbiome, omics). Radiation is the aligned midpoint.

blocks.html: The same information becomes a diagnostic when plotted as a priority-alignment map (Figure 12): literature emphasis on the horizontal axis, Decadal-priority emphasis on the vertical, with the 45° line marking perfect agreement. Points above the line are under-served — priorities want more than the literature gives — and points below are over-served. Muscle, cardiovascular, circadian, and SANS all sit clearly above the diagonal; plant/crops and microbiome sit conspicuously below it. Immune and omics sit near the line at high emphasis (aligned strengths); bone sits near the line at low emphasis (aligned neglect, with the lexical caveat noted below). The vertical distance of each bubble from the diagonal is the gap.

blocks.alt: Scatter of literature vs Decadal emphasis with 45-degree line
blocks.headline: Priority-alignment map.
blocks.caption:
Literature emphasis (x) against
  Decadal-priority emphasis (y); the dashed 45° line is perfect alignment. Bubbles above the line are
  under-served by the literature (red-tinted region); below, over-served (blue). Bubble size scales with
  the theme's OSDR emphasis. The map turns "which themes are misaligned, and how badly" into a single
  glance.

blocks.html: A natural follow-up is whether the open-data base tracks the literature or the priorities. Figure 13 plots OSDR emphasis against literature emphasis per theme. The two are strongly correlated — omics and immune are high in both, bone and cardiovascular low in both — which tells us open data is generated where the science already is, not where priorities point. The important departures are plant/crops and microbiome, which the literature emphasises but OSDR does not (they fall below the trend): these themes have bottom-up publishing momentum without a matching deposited-data substrate. Open data, in other words, inherits the literature's blind spots rather than correcting them — so it cannot be relied on to fill the human-physiology gap on its own.

blocks.alt: Scatter of literature vs OSDR emphasis per theme
blocks.headline: Open data follows the literature, not the priorities.
blocks.caption:
Per-theme OSDR
  emphasis vs. literature emphasis. The tight positive relationship means reusable data accumulates where
  publishing is already active; plant/crops and microbiome are the notable literature-rich, data-poor
  exceptions.

blocks.title: A note on Bone
paras: Bone/skeletal loss scores below average in all three corpora, which understates its true status: it is, in absolute terms, a headline physiological risk. The mean-centred probe fires weakly on strategy prose that discusses bone under broader vocabulary ("musculoskeletal countermeasures", "integrated physiology"), so bone's negative Decadal value is partly a lexical artifact. We flag it here and interpret bone in absolute terms in the discussion — a reminder that these probes are proxies, not ground truth.

blocks.html: Does the field's volume composition shift as it ages? Figure 14 answers directly: the share of each year's papers falling into each super-theme, 1995–2024. The striking result is how stable it is. The on-target space-biology/radiation band holds a remarkably steady 25–30% of output across three decades (rising modestly from ~25% to ~30%); the classic cell-biology and proteomics clusters slowly cede a few points; and — a genuine data-quality finding — the bibliographic-metadata-noise band roughly doubles from ~10% to ~19%, evidence that the OpenAlex net grows noisier over time and that de-noising is essential before any count-based claim.

blocks.alt: 100% stacked area of topic share over time
blocks.headline: Share of yearly output by topic (1995–2024).
blocks.caption: A 100%-stacked view of the nine super-themes. Coarse composition is broadly stable: the on-target band (blue) holds ~25–30% throughout, while the growing pale band at top is bibliographic-metadata noise, not science. The scientific reorientation of the field is not visible at this resolution.

blocks.html: The absolute-volume view (Figure 15) adds the other half of the picture: while shares are stable, counts grow explosively — the field roughly quadruples its annual output over the window, so a "stable share" of the on-target band still means several-fold more on-target papers per year. It also makes the noise problem vivid: the metadata-noise line is among the fastest-growing in absolute terms, a caution for anyone mining OpenAlex at scale.

blocks.alt: Absolute papers per super-theme per year
blocks.headline: Absolute output per topic cluster per year.
blocks.caption:
The same nine
  super-themes as counts rather than shares. Total output rises steeply; the on-target band grows with it,
  but so does the metadata-noise band. Toggle series in the legend to isolate a cluster's growth curve.

blocks.title: Why this matters methodologically
paras: If you counted papers per topic per year — the most common way to argue "the field is moving toward X" — you would conclude the field is standing still. It is not. The movement is in emphasis within the on-target literature, which only the semantic probe of §4.4 can see. Volume is the wrong instrument for this question.

blocks.text: Semantic emphasis over time: the divergence

blocks.html: Applying the mean-centred probe year by year to the literature exposes the motion the composition chart hides. Figure 16 tracks all ten risk themes from 1995 to 2024. The lines fan apart into two diverging bundles. Rising: plant/crops climbs fastest of all (Δ +20.6 over the window, crossing from strongly negative to strongly positive), followed by microbiome (Δ +12.1), gene-expression/omics (Δ +4.9, from an already-high base), immune (+2.9), and circadian (+3.1). Falling: bone drops hardest (Δ −15.2), then radiation (−8.5, from a high base), muscle (−8.1), neuro-ocular/SANS (−7.0), and cardiovascular (−4.8, already the lowest).

blocks.alt: Per-year semantic emphasis of ten themes
blocks.headline: Semantic emphasis trajectories, 1995–2024.
blocks.caption:
Mean-centred emphasis of each
  risk theme, per year, in the literature. The field pulls apart into a rising bundle (plant, microbiome,
  omics, immune) and a falling bundle (bone, radiation, muscle, SANS, cardiovascular). Use the legend to
  isolate individual themes.

blocks.html:
Figure 17 ranks the net movement — the momentum of each theme over the three decades — and makes
the two bundles unmistakable. The bar sorts from plant/crops (+20.6) and microbiome (+12.1) at the top
to radiation (−8.5) and bone (−15.2) at the bottom, with the integrative human-physiology risks
clustered on the falling side.

blocks.alt: Temporal momentum ranked by theme
blocks.headline: Momentum, ranked.
blocks.caption:
Change in literature emphasis from 1995–99 to
  2020–24 for each theme. Positive = rising attention; negative = falling. The molecular/plant themes
  gain; the integrative human-physiology risks lose.

blocks.html: The single most legible reversal is radiation versus plant/crops (Figure 18). In the late 1990s, radiation was among the most-emphasised themes and plant biology among the least; the lines converge through the 2000s and cross around 2013, after which plant/crops climbs well above radiation. Two themes central to a Mars mission — protecting the crew from cosmic rays, and growing their food — literally trade places in the literature's attention, in the direction opposite to what a countermeasure-driven agency would choose. §5 asks what drove each line.

blocks.alt: Radiation vs plant emphasis crossover
blocks.headline: A reversal, isolated.
blocks.caption:
Space-radiation and plant/crop emphasis in the
  literature, 1995–2024. Radiation starts high and declines; plant/crops starts low and climbs, overtaking
  radiation around 2013. The crossing is the report's central empirical claim in miniature.

blocks.html: Figure 19 isolates the six themes that matter most for the mission argument, showing the same crossing among the human-physiology risks and the molecular/plant risers together. The literature is, measurably, reorienting away from integrative human physiology and toward molecular and plant biology.

blocks.alt: Focused six-theme widening gap chart
blocks.headline: The widening gap (focused).
blocks.caption:
Six themes from Figure 16: rising
  plant/crops and omics against falling bone, cardiovascular, muscle, and SANS. The crossing lines are
  the report's central empirical claim.

blocks.html:
The static gap (§4.2) and the temporal momentum (§4.4) are independent axes, and a theme's situation
is defined by both. Figure 20 crosses them: the vertical axis is how much more the priorities want
a theme than the literature supplies (Decadal − Literature emphasis); the horizontal axis is which way
the literature is moving. The four quadrants have sharp meanings.

blocks.alt: Quadrant scatter of priority gap versus momentum
blocks.headline: The synthesis map.
blocks.caption: Priority−literature gap (vertical) against temporal momentum (horizontal) for all ten themes; bubble size scales with the theme's absolute literature emphasis. Red (upper-left) = under-served and falling; green (lower-right) = over-served and rising.

blocks.html: The upper-left "danger" quadrant — under-served and falling — contains exactly the integrative human-physiology risks: muscle, cardiovascular, neuro-ocular/SANS, and radiation. These are themes the Decadal Survey weights above the literature, whose literature emphasis is nonetheless dropping. The lower-right "momentum-without-pull" quadrant — over-served and rising — contains omics, microbiome, and plant/crops: themes the literature is racing toward with neither a priority mandate nor (for plant and microbiome) a strong open-data base beneath them. Immune and circadian sit in the benign "under-served but rising" quadrant (catching up); bone sits in the lower-left, dragged there by the lexical artifact noted in §4.2 but unambiguously a top absolute risk that is falling fast. No theme sits where NASA would most want them — the upper-right, high-priority and rising.

blocks.text: What each corpus actually says: phrase fingerprints

blocks.html: Bigram frequencies confirm the identities behind the numbers. OSDR (Figure 21) is transcriptomics plus experimental design — "gene expression", "rna seq", "differentially expressed", "simulated microgravity", "ground control", "nasa genelab". The Decadal Survey (Figure 22) is strategic and cross-disciplinary — "physical sciences" is its single most frequent bigram, ahead of "space exploration" and "future space". Most revealing is the literature's own plant super-theme (Figure 23): its top phrases are "arabidopsis thaliana", "genome editing", "internal transcribed spacer" (a DNA-barcoding marker), and phylogenetics vocabulary — this is foundational plant genomics, not applied crop production for life support. The rising plant literature of Figure 16 is not, at the phrase level, the bioregenerative-food-system research a Mars mission needs.

blocks.alt: OSDR top bigrams
blocks.headline: OSDR phrase fingerprint.
blocks.caption:
Transcriptomics and standardised experimental
  design dominate — the vocabulary of reusable mechanistic evidence.

blocks.alt: Decadal top bigrams
blocks.headline: Decadal phrase fingerprint.
blocks.caption:
"Physical sciences" leads; the register is
  strategic and forward-looking, spanning disciplines beyond biology.

blocks.alt: Space biology plant super-theme top bigrams
blocks.headline: The plant surge, up close.
blocks.caption: The literature's plant super-theme is Arabidopsis genomics, genome editing, and DNA-barcode phylogenetics — foundational plant science, not applied crop production. The distinction is decisive for the funding argument.

blocks.text: The connective tissue: which risks are studied together

blocks.html: The analysis so far has treated the ten risk themes as independent columns. They are not. A paper on cardiovascular deconditioning is disproportionately likely to also discuss muscle and fluid shifts; a spaceflight transcriptomics paper routinely touches radiation-induced DNA damage. To map this connective tissue we take the on-target literature (the 4,415 papers scoring above the relevance floor) and, for each paper, its ten theme-probe scores. Subtracting each paper's own mean across the ten themes removes the dominant “how on-topic is this paper at all” factor, leaving a relative-emphasis profile; correlating those profiles across papers answers a sharper question — when a paper leans toward one theme, which others does it lean toward with it? Figure 24 shows the resulting 10×10 structure.

blocks.alt: Correlation heatmap of the ten risk themes
blocks.headline: Which risks share papers.
blocks.caption: Within-paper co-emphasis correlation of the ten risk themes across the on-target literature (n = 4,415), ordered by hierarchical clustering. Warm (red) = studied together; cool (blue) = traded off. Three blocks emerge on the diagonal. Hover any cell for the exact coefficient.

blocks.html: Three blocks sit on the diagonal. A tight integrative-human-physiology block — muscle, cardiovascular, neuro-ocular/SANS, circadian, and immune — co-occurs internally (muscle–cardiovascular r = 0.54 is the strongest positive in the matrix). A molecular block links gene-expression/omics to radiation/DNA (r = 0.31) and to bone (0.33) — the signature of mechanism-of-injury studies. And a small organismal block pairs plant/crops with microbiome (0.40). Between the blocks the correlations turn sharply negative — muscle vs. microbiome r = −0.57, plant vs. immune −0.44 — because a paper devoted to plant genomics is, by construction, not a paper about human muscle.

blocks.alt: Force-directed co-occurrence network of the ten themes
blocks.headline: The field's risk communities.
blocks.caption: The same correlations as a force-directed network: green edges join themes studied together (r > 0.2), faint red dotted edges mark the strongest trade-offs (r < −0.33), node colour encodes 30-year momentum (red falling, green rising) and node size the theme's literature emphasis. Greedy modularity recovers three communities.

blocks.html: Rendering the same matrix as a network (Figure 25) makes the report's thesis visible in a single image. Community detection — greedy modularity on the positive edges — returns exactly three groups: {muscle, cardiovascular, SANS, circadian, immune}, {bone, omics, radiation}, and {plant, microbiome}. Colour the nodes by momentum and the alignment is stark: the integrative-human-physiology community is almost uniformly warm — it is the falling bundle — while the organismal community glows green. The falling risks are not ten independent declines that happen to point the same way; they are one densely-connected community of co-studied problems retreating together. That is a stronger and more worrying statement than the marginal trajectories alone: the field is not turning away from muscle and cardiovascular and ocular risk separately, it is turning away from the integrative-physiology cluster as a whole — exactly the cluster whose members fail together on a long mission.

blocks.title: The falling bundle is one community
paras: Modularity analysis of theme co-occurrence recovers the integrative-human-physiology risks (muscle, cardiovascular, neuro-ocular, circadian, immune) as a single connected community — and it is the community whose 30-year momentum is negative across the board. Their shared decline is one reorientation of the field, not a coincidence of ten. A risk community this tightly coupled is also, physiologically, the set of systems a Mars transit destabilises at once.

blocks.text: Is the divergence slowing? An acceleration view

blocks.html: A widening gap could still be decelerating — the field could be in the act of correcting. To check, we split each theme's 30-year momentum into an early half (mean emphasis 1995–99 → 2015–19) and a recent half (2015–19 → 2020–24) and plot one against the other (Figure 26). The recent axis is the decision-relevant one: it says which way each theme is moving now. The news is not reassuring. Bone has the most negative recent momentum of any theme — it is not merely low, it is still falling fastest; radiation, muscle, and cardiovascular remain in the still-falling quadrant. Two encouraging signals do appear: neuro-ocular/SANS crosses into slightly-positive recent momentum, consistent with the emerging-risk reading of §5 (its specialised literature is finally growing), and gene-expression/omics has flattened to essentially zero recent momentum — it has matured into stable infrastructure rather than continuing to crowd out other work. Plant and microbiome are still accelerating upward. In short, the reorientation identified over three decades has not begun to reverse in the most recent five years; if anything the human-physiology risks are still losing ground.

blocks.alt: Scatter of early vs recent momentum for the ten themes
blocks.headline: Still moving the wrong way.
blocks.caption: Each theme's early momentum (1995–99 → 2015–19 emphasis change) against its recent momentum (2015–19 → 2020–24); colour is the full 30-year change. Points in the lower-left are still falling — the human-physiology risks sit there, with bone the most negative on the recent axis. Omics has plateaued (matured); SANS has just crossed to slightly rising.

blocks.text: Reading the trajectories against the historical record

blocks.html: A drift in emphasis is only interesting if it has causes. To test whether the movements of §4.4 are noise or signal, we assembled a timeline of the programmes, facilities, funding initiatives, and landmark publications that a domain reader would expect to move each theme, and checked it against the trajectories. The correspondence is close enough that most of the major inflections have a plausible external driver — and, importantly, the drivers of the falls differ in kind from the drivers of the rises.

blocks.alt: Emphasis trajectories annotated with real-world events
blocks.headline: The timeline, drawn.
blocks.caption: Five representative themes with the programmes, facilities, and landmark publications of the timeline overlaid as dated markers. Every date shown was verified against a primary source (see the validation table below). The molecular and plant rises begin near their triggering events; the bone and radiation declines run through the maturation of their countermeasures and facilities, not the closure of the risk.

blocks.html: The rises are technology- and landmark-driven. Gene-expression/omics holds the highest emphasis throughout and rises further, which is exactly what one expects from a theme carried by a falling cost of sequencing and by dedicated infrastructure: NASA GeneLab launched in 2014 and consolidated into OSDR in 2021,1 and the 2019 Twins Study — NASA's first integrated human multi-omics investigation, published in Science2 — gave the molecular turn a canonical, heavily-cited exemplar. Microbiome's Δ +12 rise begins in earnest in the 2010s, lagging the NIH Human Microbiome Project (funded 2007, landmark results 2012), which catalysed a roughly forty-fold increase in microbiome research funding across NIH7 and supplied both the methods and the framing that space biology then applied to the ISS and to the Twins Study's gut-microbiome findings. Plant/crops — the fastest riser, crossing zero around 2004 and overtaking radiation around 2013 (Fig 18) — coincides with the operational plant programme on the ISS: the Veggie chamber (2014) and the first space-grown food eaten by astronauts (2015), and the automated Advanced Plant Habitat (2018).3 Yet the phrase fingerprint (Fig 23) shows the published plant surge is dominated by Arabidopsis genomics and DNA-barcoding, not by the applied food-production science the flight hardware was built for — the literature rode the visibility of the milestones with the tools it already had.

One of these drivers is quantifiable, and it is not specific to space biology at all. The molecular turn rides the collapse in the cost of DNA sequencing: NHGRI's cost-per-genome fell from roughly $95 million in 2001 to about $525 by 2022, with the discontinuity of next-generation sequencing compressing a decade of Moore's-law decline into 2008 alone.10 Overlaying that curve on the omics and microbiome emphasis trajectories (Figure 28) shows the rise tracking the fall in cost — a field-wide tide, imported from biomedicine at large, that lifted omics everywhere and that space biology rode with the tools it already had. It reinforces §6.5's reading: omics is not a space-biology priority that won on the merits of the mission, it is a general-purpose method made cheap, and the right response is to aim it at the under-served risks rather than to read its momentum as a signal of where the science should go.

blocks.alt: Sequencing cost overlaid on omics and microbiome emphasis
blocks.headline: The molecular tide is exogenous.
blocks.caption: Omics and microbiome emphasis in the literature (left axis) against NHGRI cost-per-genome (right axis, log, inverted). The molecular rise coincides with a roughly 100,000-fold collapse in sequencing cost — an external driver shared with all of biology, not a mission-specific pull. Microbiome's rise additionally lags the NIH Human Microbiome Project (2007 funding, 2012 landmark results).

blocks.html: The falls are maturation- and measurement-driven — not resolution. This is the crucial asymmetry. Radiation's decline from a high base follows, rather than precedes, the field's institutionalisation: the NSRL opened in 20034 and the Mars-transit dose was directly measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument in 201311 — the questions became better-defined and better-resourced, so undifferentiated "radiation" language in the broad literature declined even as the risk itself did not. Bone's steep fall is the clearest "false-solved" case: the ARED resistive-exercise device (which flew on the ISS in 2008) combined with bisphosphonate protocols was shown to largely preserve bone mineral density over six-month missions,6 and as the countermeasure matured through 2013 the emphasis dropped — even though post-flight recovery of bone remains incomplete and Mars-duration exposure far exceeds the six-month evidence base. Most subtle is SANS: it was only first described in 2011 (as VIIP, renamed SANS c.2017),5 so it is a genuinely emerging risk — yet our broad-net probe shows its emphasis falling. The most likely explanation is a measurement one: the specialised, recent SANS clinical literature is small and lexically specific, and a broad OpenAlex harvest with a generic probe under-captures it. The honest reading is therefore doubly concerning — SANS is probably more active than our trajectory shows, but it is still badly under-represented in the broad literature relative to a risk that did not exist as a named entity twenty years ago and now shapes mission medical planning.

blocks.title: The asymmetry that matters
paras: The themes that rose did so because a technology, a landmark result, or a flagship experiment pulled the community in (GeneLab, the Twins Study, the Human Microbiome Project, Veggie). The themes that fell did so because their countermeasures and facilities matured — creating an impression of "handled" — not because the underlying risk was closed. A research portfolio that lets attention follow novelty away from maturing-but-unsolved risks is exactly backwards for a Mars-duration mission, where those risks compound.

blocks.html: External validation. Because the interpretive weight of this section rests on the timeline being correct, every date and quantitative claim in it was checked against a primary or authoritative source. All held, with a single refinement — the resistive-exercise hardware flew in 2008, not the mid-2000s development date sometimes cited. Two figures worth stating in full emerged from the check: NASA's Biological and Physical Sciences division ran on about $85 million in FY2023 against the Decadal Survey's recommended ~$1 billion,9 and non-HMP microbiome funding at NIH rose more than forty-fold after 2007.7 The table records the verification.

blocks.html: Six connected patterns emerge when the static, temporal, and historical views are read together.

6.1 — The gap is two-dimensional, and it is widening. Under-service and negative momentum coincide. The very themes the Decadal Survey elevates above current literature (muscle, cardiovascular, SANS) are the themes whose literature emphasis is falling (Figure 20, red quadrant). A gap that were merely static might close on its own; a gap that is static and widening will not. This is the report's central finding, and it is specifically about integrative human physiology — the systems that fail together on a long mission.

6.2 — Volume hides the shift. Coarse composition is stable (Figure 14) while semantic emphasis diverges (Figure 16). A field can look motionless by paper count while quietly reorienting its attention. Any research-portfolio audit that counts outputs rather than measuring emphasis will miss exactly this kind of drift.

6.3 — Falls signal maturation, not closure. The event grounding (§5) shows the declining themes fell as their countermeasures and facilities matured — ARED and bisphosphonates for bone, NSRL and the RAD dose measurement for radiation — not because the risks were solved. Emphasis is a proxy for attention, and attention rationally leaves a problem that looks handled; but "handled for six months in LEO" is not "handled for three years to Mars". The falling bundle is where a mission-driven funder should be most alert to the difference between fashion and closure.

6.4 — The crop-science triple bind. Plant/crops is the fastest-rising theme in the literature, yet it is priority-light (Decadal −11.4), open-data-poor (OSDR −9.3, and below the corpus-correlation trend in Fig 13), and — at the phrase level — foundational Arabidopsis genomics rather than applied crop production (Figure 23). It is simultaneously the field's greatest bottom-up momentum and its least-coordinated: energy without a mission channel or a reusable-data substrate. The ISS already flies the hardware (Veggie, Advanced Plant Habitat); the gap is between the flight programme's applied intent and the literature's genomic reflex. This is an opportunity, not a criticism — momentum this strong is exactly what targeted coordination can convert into mission capability.

6.5 — Omics is a method, not a mission. Gene-expression/omics is the highest-emphasis theme in both the literature and OSDR, but lower in the Decadal Survey, because the survey organises priorities by risk and system whereas omics is a technique that serves all of them. Omics is not a gap; it is the shared instrument — and the "NASA GeneLab RNA-seq consensus pipeline" (Figure 21) plus the Twins Study's multi-omics design show the community already treats it as infrastructure. The corpus-correlation result (Fig 13) reinforces this: open data pools where the molecular methods already are. The implication is to fund omics as infrastructure pointed at the under-served risks, not as an open-ended science area.

6.6 — Radiation is slipping from a strong base. Radiation is priority-relevant (its gap is near zero, Fig 11) and the best-datafied risk in OSDR, yet its literature emphasis is falling (Δ −8.5). Unlike bone (thin and falling) this is a well-resourced area losing momentum — a "protect the lead" case rather than a "rescue" case, but still a warning for a beyond-LEO programme where radiation is unavoidable and, per the RAD measurement, quantified but not mitigated.

6.7 — The neglected risks form a community, which makes the drift coherent rather than accidental. The co-occurrence analysis (§4.7) shows the falling themes — muscle, cardiovascular, neuro-ocular, circadian — are a single densely-connected cluster the literature studies together, and the acceleration view (§4.8) shows that cluster is still losing emphasis in the most recent five years. A drift spread across ten unrelated topics might be noise; a coordinated retreat from one coherent community of co-studied, mutually-compounding physiological risks is a structural signal. It is also the community a Mars transit stresses simultaneously — which is why the connectivity matters operationally, not just statistically.

The analysis is correlational and its probes are proxies (§8), so what follows is a hypothesis, not a directive. But the evidence points one way with unusual consistency: NASA's research funding should move counter-cyclically to the literature's drift, anchoring on Decadal priorities and mission criticality rather than on where publications are already flowing. The 2023 Decadal Survey's own finding — that BPS is the least-funded division in the Science Mission Directorate and needs roughly a ten-fold increase9 — means the practical question is less "what to cut" than "where new money should land first." Concretely:

rows.html: ▲ Fund more
Integrative human physiology — cardiovascular/fluid-shift, neuro-ocular/SANS, muscle, bone

The "danger" quadrant (Fig 20): priority-elevated yet under-served and falling (Δ −4.8 to −15.2). Falls track countermeasure maturation, not closure (§5). Mission-critical for Mars-class durations; thin in OSDR.
▲ Fund more
Integrated / translational & countermeasure studies (analog- and ISS-based, multi-system)

The Decadal Survey explicitly calls for integrated translational research; the falling themes are precisely the interacting systems such studies address, and the six-month countermeasure evidence base must be extended to Mars durations.
▲ Fund more
Applied bioregenerative crop production + plant open-data infrastructure

Redirect the strong plant momentum (Fig 16, 18) from Arabidopsis genomics (Fig 23) toward the food-system science the ISS hardware (Veggie, APH) was built for, and require OSDR crop-data deposition (the triple bind, §6.4).
◆ Sustain / protect
Space radiation; immune dysregulation
Radiation: aligned (Fig 11) and well-datafied but momentum slipping — protect it; the dose is measured but not mitigated. Immune: aligned and healthily rising — steady support.
◆ Fund as infrastructure
Omics / GeneLab-OSDR pipelines & data standards

Omics is the shared method (§6.5), already treated as infrastructure; open data pools where methods already are (Fig 13). Fund it pointed at the human-physiology gaps, not as a standalone growth area.
▼ Redirect (not cut)
Undirected foundational molecular/plant biology not anchored to a spaceflight risk
The literature already supplies this abundantly and it is rising on its own (Fig 16); marginal NASA dollars earn more in the under-served integrative risks.
▼ Invest instead in curation
Corpus / data quality (not a science cut)
The metadata-noise share doubled to ~19% and grows fast in absolute terms (Fig 14, 15); better curation raises the return on every other investment.

blocks.title: The one-sentence hypothesis
paras: Shift marginal research funding toward the integrative human-physiology risks that deep-space missions make unavoidable — cardiovascular/fluid-shift, neuro-ocular/SANS, muscle, and bone — because the literature is retreating from them as their countermeasures merely mature at exactly the moment the mission needs them extended to Mars durations, and convert the field's existing omics and plant momentum into infrastructure and applied capability aimed at those same risks.

items: Proxies, not outcomes. Semantic emphasis measures research attention, not funding, quality, or result. High emphasis need not mean a risk is solved, nor low emphasis that it is ignored in practice — the SANS case (§5) shows a real, growing risk that the broad-net probe under-captures.

Relative, within-corpus metric. Mean-centering answers "relative to this corpus's own average"; it cannot compare absolute levels across corpora. Bone (§4.2) shows how a narrow lexical probe can understate a risk discussed under other vocabulary — domain judgement is required.
Literature-only time axis. OSDR dates are corrupted (epoch bug) and the Decadal volumes are undated, so all temporal claims describe the published literature, not the priorities or the data base.

Event grounding is associational. The §5 timeline establishes plausibility and temporal coincidence, not causation; other factors (journal launches, adjacent-field spillover, funding cycles we did not model) also move emphasis.
A noisy net. The OpenAlex harvest is broad and >99% low-relevance, with a rising metadata-noise fraction; all count-based statements are corrected for relevance but residual noise remains.
Hand-specified probes and correlational design. The ten themes and their query wordings are chosen, not learned, and no causal claim is made about why the literature drifts.

blocks.html: Placing NASA's stated priorities, its open-data evidence, and its published literature in one shared semantic space turns an unanswerable qualitative worry — "is space biology studying the right things?" — into a measurable one. The answer is a qualified no with a clear direction. The field is aligned and strong where it is molecular (omics, immune); it is drifting where it is integrative and human (cardiovascular, ocular, muscular, skeletal). That drift is invisible to paper-counting and only appears when emphasis is measured; it is not static but widening; and — read against the historical record — it reflects attention following new tools and flagship results toward the molecular, while leaving the human-physiology risks behind precisely as their countermeasures looked handled. The rising energy in the field — plant biology, microbiome, omics — is real and valuable but currently points away from the mission and lacks the open-data substrate to be reused. With the Decadal Survey itself calling the programme severely under-funded, the opportunity for NASA is to spend counter-cyclically: to pull the integrative human-physiology risks back up the agenda, extend their six-month countermeasure evidence to Mars durations, and convert the field's molecular momentum into the infrastructure and applied capability a crewed Mars mission will require.

Reproducibility. All figures are generated by the Research-Gap Identification platform from three corpora: Space_Biology (101,273 OpenAlex records), OSDR (171 open-data papers / 8,646 chunks), and Decadal_Survey (3 National Academies volumes / 2,580 passages). Pipeline: SPECTER2 embeddings → UMAP → HDBSCAN topic discovery → keyword labelling; hierarchical structure via topic-centroid Ward linkage (hierarchical_dendrogram / hierarchical_cluster); cross-corpus comparison via combined-corpus semantic scoring with per-corpus mean-centering; temporal views via per-year share and per-year mean emphasis (literature only). Emphasis values are mean-centred and scaled ×1000. This document embeds every chart as a live Plotly figure together with a single copy of the plotting library, so it is fully self-contained and interactive offline.
